title: Contextual Shotcraft — quick notes & experiments
body:
Purpose:
Quick personal scratchpad for experiments around variable-context few-shot templates. Trying to balance anchor examples, negative examples, and short instructions so models preserve task intent across rollouts and quantized variants. Not polished — notes to self + snippets to copy into eval harness.

High-level goals:
- Build compact few-shot sets that are robust when context window shrinks (e.g., when using 4k -> 2k tokens).
- Surface brittle failure modes (instruction drift, hallucinated attributes, repetition) and capture minimal counterexamples.
- Create template variants that are cheap (token-wise) but maintain high signal for downstream heuristics and auto-eval.

Observations so far:
- Anchored examples (explicit role + output format) help with preserving structure; but too many anchor examples cause parroting of exact wording.
- Negative examples ("bad output" annotated) reduce overconfident hallucination on entity synthesis tasks, but increase verbosity in safe trials.
- Models on quantized hosts (int8/4-bit) amplify token-level jitter; prefer shorter demonstration labels and consistent separators.
- When temperature > 0.6, few-shot ordering becomes more important than content; randomizing shot order in training helps but is terrible for deterministic evals.

Shot patterns to try (names to use in harness):
1) Anchor-Compact (3 examples) — each example: role line, input, output, 1-line rationale (optional).
2) Contrast-Pair (2 pos / 2 neg) — show one correct approach and one common mistake per input type.
3) Micro-Rubric (1 example + 1 rubric line) — heavy on formatting constraints, e.g., JSON schema.
4) Progressive (4 examples) — increasing difficulty; includes a final truncated example to simulate context cut.

Example templates (keep token budget in mind):
- Anchor-Compact:
  ===
  System: You are a helpful assistant that returns a JSON with keys: summary, important_facts
  Input: "Summarize the user email below."
  Example 1:
  Input: "Hi team, need deploy by EOW. Blocks: failing tests, db migration."
  Output: {"summary":"Deploy deadline EOW; blockers: failing tests, db migration","important_facts":["deadline: EOW","blockers: tests, db migration"]}
  ===
  (2 more examples)

- Contrast-Pair (short):
  ===
  Good -> Input: "Extract customer asks and priority"
  Output: "asks:[...], priority: high"
  Bad -> Input: "Extract customer asks and priority"
  Output: "The customer wants a promo and is upset. Also thinks product is slow."  # missing structured fields
  ===

Negative examples design notes:
- Keep negative examples semantically plausible but structurally wrong (e.g., wrong keys, extra commentary).
- Attach a short tag: [NEG] so harness can detect and compute false-positive rate on structural checks.
- Use negative examples sparingly (1 per 3 positive) — too many negatives push the model to be defensive and add hedging language.

Failure catalog (to grow):
- Instruction drift: model obeys earlier general instruction but ignores format spec in last shot.
  Trigger: long natural-language rationale in example 3.
  Mitigation: move format spec to SYSTEM line and repeat at end shortened.

- Hallucinated-names: model invents person names when inputs are vague.
  Trigger: short input with pronouns only.
  Mitigation: provide explicit 'if missing, return null' rule in rubric.

- Repetition loop on quantized deploys: repeated sentence fragments at end of output.
  Trigger: high token-per-second throughput + batching.
  Mitigation: add explicit 'do not repeat' guard and post-process trim in serving layer.

Quick experiments to run (metrics we capture) — run on hosted and dedicated variants:
- Structural pass rate (% outputs parse to expected JSON schema)
- Hallucination count (named entities not present in input) per 1000 outputs
- Token overhead (avg tokens per output) compared to baseline template
- Latency delta at 95th pctl when adding negative examples in prompt

Pseudocode for harness snippet (informal):
- shots = [selected template shots]
- prompt = system_line + '\n'.join(shots)+ '\nInput: '+user_text
- response = call_model(prompt, temp=0.2)
- parse_ok = try_parse_json(response)
- if not parse_ok: classify_failure(response)
- record tokens, latency, parse_ok

Mini-experiments & quick results (scratch runs on 2024-12-15):
- Anchor-Compact (3 shots) on 13B quantized: structure pass 82%, hallucination 11 per 1000, avg tokens 92
- Contrast-Pair (2pos/2neg) on 7B hosted: structure pass 75%, hallucination 6 per 1000, avg tokens 114 (negatives increased verbosity)
- Micro-Rubric (1 shot + rubric) on 13B hosted: structure pass 90%, avg tokens 78, but occasional terse outputs missing optional fields

Notes to self / TODOs:
- Add a mini-eval comparing shot-order vs static rubric-only for quantized models (ENG-1123 ticket).
- Try 'separator token' variants: '---' vs '\n\n' vs '###' — measure parse_ok changes.
- Build a tiny synthetic negative generator to automatically craft common mistakes for each input class.
- Share top-3 prompts with Marco for replication in the eval pool; ask Evelyn to add structural schema checks to the pipeline.

Potential deliverables for end of month:
- 6 compact templates (two per pattern above) + results table (structure pass / hallucination / token overhead)
- Integration PR to add parse_ok metric to nightly evals (link in linked_artifacts)

Random scribbles (keep):
- "If the input contains 'we', ask clarifying Q unless explicit instruction says not to."
- Try swapping the order: example outputs before example inputs (weirdly sometimes increases terse JSON output) — add as small ablation.

Bottom line: keep token budget tight. Use micro-rubrics where possible for quantized hosts. Capture negative cases early so rollout doesn't regress downstream parsers.
